problem: Sim-to-real end-to-end visual navigation policies trained in coarse simulators fail in the real world because the input representation (RGB, depth, segmentation) is either too appearance-dependent or ignores real sensor noise. No systematic way exists to compare or design representations.
motivation: Real-world data collection for end-to-end navigation is costly, and mobile-robot environments are too diverse to simulate finely, so the representation must carry navigation-relevant information while shrinking the sim-real gap. The authors observe that human operators abstract spatial and semantic information from RGB, and that low-level intensity/texture differs most between sim and real.
key_idea: Use a representation that explicitly combines spatial information (depth image with an embedded real-sensor noise model) and semantic information (a risk-categorized YOLO detection image), fed through two separate encoders, to enable sim-to-real imitation-learned navigation.
insight: Explicitly encoding high-level spatial and semantic information, while excluding appearance and embedding the real sensor noise, is what makes transfer work. In simulation, noise-free depth had 5.6 interventions versus 0.6 with the noise model. In the real world, only the two noise-embedded models worked, and the ones without noise stayed still or kept steering. RGB noise augmentation hurt (46.0 interventions), and feature maps show the RGB model responds to appearance rather than to geometry or pedestrians.
method: VIP model and criteria: Abstraction pyramid from intensity/texture to spatial/semantic information; three criteria: explicit spatial and semantic information, little intensity/texture, and a noise model M with ||M(E_sim)-E_real||→0.

Noisy depth: Gaussian noise on Canny-detected object edges (Kinect V2 model σ(z)=(0.0012+0.0019(z-0.4)^2)·ξ, ξ∈[1,1.2]), random border masking (Gaussian+uniform, 0-30% of pixels), plus salt-and-pepper noise.

Categorized detection image: YOLOv3 detections graded into 6 collision-risk categories and drawn as a gray-scale image (higher risk means higher intensity, pedestrians highest; higher-risk objects win on overlap).

Two-encoder network: Encoder 1 for depth (dense layers of 480 units), Encoder 2 for the detection image (dense layers of 32 units), concatenated with a one-hot direction command (forward/left/right/stop) and passed through 3 dense layers to output v and ω. Input is 256×192; runs at over 20 Hz.
Imitation learning: Expert FPV joystick data (1 hour, Gazebo indoor) with randomly initialized recovery situations, MSE loss on v and ω plus L2, Adam, batch size 40, lr 1e-4, 400 epochs, dropout 0.5.
Feature-map evaluation: Average the channels of the middle conv layer on real RGB-D observations to visualize the network's reaction to obstacles, as a fast pre-test.

setting.backbone: Small CNN encoders + dense layers (trained from scratch, imitation learning); YOLOv3 detector for the semantic image
setting.training_data: 1 hour of expert joystick FPV demonstrations in a coarse Gazebo indoor environment, including recovery samples
setting.observation: Monocular first-person RGB-D (Kinect V2), 256x192 depth plus YOLOv3 categorized detection image, plus a discrete global direction command
setting.privileged: none (direction commands at intersections sent by joystick; ground-truth velocity used only for evaluation in simulation)

numbers_note: No standard benchmark; custom Gazebo and real-lab tests. Results (interventions, time, velocity decrease, score) are in Tables 1-2 and do not map to canonical navigation benchmarks, so they are omitted from numbers.
results: In simulated testing, the full representation (noisy depth + categorized detection) had 0.2 interventions vs 5.6 for noise-free depth, 2.5 for RGB, and 26.7-32.7 for segmentation baselines. In a 90 m real corridor with pedestrians, it averaged 0.8 interventions (subjective score 4.0/5) and 12.2% velocity decrease near pedestrians, while the other baselines exceeded 20 interventions.
limitations: Small evaluation (12 simulated and 5 real trials per model) with a single training simulator and a 1-hour dataset; no standard benchmark.
Depends on a hand-designed sensor noise model specific to Kinect V2, and on YOLO detections with manual risk categories.
Imitation learning only, with goal directions supplied by a joystick and no global planning; RL is left for future work.
compares_to: E_RGB / RGB with noise augmentation (Conditional Affordance Learning)
